title: Holy Thursday
hookLine: the Mass of the Lord's Supper, washing of feet, and the altar stripped bare

cards: Thursday evening, the last week before Easter. The parish church fills for an evening Mass, and something is off. The tabernacle behind the altar stands open, and it's empty.
Then the Gloria begins, and the bells ring out: the little altar bells, sometimes the tower bell too, with the organ at full. Then the bells stop. They won't ring again until Saturday night.
A little later the priest takes off his outer vestment, ties a towel around his waist, and kneels on the floor in front of a row of people with their shoes off.

teach.b: Triduum is Latin for three days. The Church keeps everything from Thursday evening to Sunday evening as one single celebration, counted evening to evening, from this evening Mass to evening prayer on Easter Sunday.

Tonight is called the Mass of the Lord's Supper. It remembers the last meal Jesus ate with his friends, and Catholics say two gifts were given at that table: the Eucharist, and the priesthood that celebrates it.
Then the strange part. In John's Gospel, during that supper, Jesus gets up, takes a towel, and washes his disciples' feet, a servant's job. Peter won't have it.

teach.h: THOU SHALT NEVER WASH MY FEET.
teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims he says, "Thou shalt never wash my feet." Jesus tells him that unless he is washed, he has no part with him.
Afterward Jesus says, "If then I being your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; you also ought to wash one another's feet."
In English this night is often called Maundy Thursday, and maundy is usually traced to the Latin mandatum, a commandment, from what Jesus says that night: "A new commandment I give unto you."
At the end there's no blessing and no dismissal.
The priest carries the Eucharist in procession to a side altar while the church sings, and the main altar is stripped bare: cloths, candles, flowers, all gone.
People stay and keep watch, sometimes until midnight, answering the question from the garden: could you not watch one hour?

how: Catholics celebrate the evening Mass of the Lord's Supper on Holy Thursday; in many parishes the priest washes the feet of chosen parishioners, and afterward people keep watch in prayer before the Eucharist at a side altar, often called the altar of repose.

a three-day fast kept before Easter

s: Holy Thursday Mass ends with the usual blessing and dismissal
there's no dismissal. the Eucharist is carried to a side altar, and the main altar is stripped bare.
the bells ring at the Gloria, then stay silent until the Easter Vigil
every bell rings at once, and then they wait until Saturday night.
in John's Gospel, Peter gladly lets Jesus wash his feet
he refused at first: thou shalt never wash my feet.

games.q: you're Peter. your teacher kneels in front of you with a towel and a basin to wash your feet. what do you do?
o: refuse: he will never wash your feet.
offer to wash his feet instead.
games.why: Peter refused. Jesus told him that unless he was washed he would have no part with him, and then Peter asked him to wash his hands and his head too.

practice: Picture washing something for someone, slowly, the way a servant would, without being thanked: a sink of someone else's dishes, a child's hands, a friend's muddy boots, the mug at work that isn't yours.
Notice any part of you that says, like Peter, not me, not that. If you pray, bring that part to God; if you don't, just stay with the picture of your hands in the water.

wordCard.voice: Triduum. Three days, from Thursday night to Sunday night, kept as one feast of his death and rising. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: a space of three days. the full name is the Paschal Triduum, the three days of the passover.

carryVoice: Your line: the three holiest days begin. A supper, a towel, a bare altar, a long watch. See you tomorrow.
